title: Event logs and the Alpha algorithm

cards.question: Which kinds of questions can event logs help answer?
cards.answer: For example when and how many process instances were executed, which activity sequences are frequent, and whether a model contains behavior that was never executed.
distractors: Which employees should be hired next year and at what salary.
What the legal definition of a business process is.
How to translate a Petri net into source code.

cards.question: Why are logs a good basis for evidence-based answers about a process?
cards.answer: They are not biased by human perception of how the process is run, nor by fragmented process knowledge, provided that data quality is high.
distractors: They always contain every possible behavior of the process.
They are guaranteed to be free of noise.
They contain a formal model that is verified by the process owner.

cards.question: What is a case in an event log?
cards.answer: A process instance, consisting of events that all relate to that one case and that are ordered.
distractors: A single activity type in the process model.
A set of all events of one resource.
A place in a Petri net with a token.

cards.question: What is the structure of an event log, from top to bottom?
cards.answer: A log is a collection of cases, each case is a sequence (trace) of events, and each event has attributes.
distractors: A log is a set of activities, each activity is a set of cases, and each case has one event.
A log is a single trace made of cases.
A log is a set of events, with cases being optional attributes of the log.

cards.question: How many cases can a single event relate to?
cards.answer: Precisely one.
distractors: Any number of cases.
At least two cases.
None; cases are attributes of the log.

cards.question: Which attributes does each event need at minimum, according to the event log terminology?
cards.answer: A case id, an activity and a point in time.
distractors: A resource, a cost and a location.
A transition, a place and a marking.
A model name and a version number.

cards.question: Name typical event attribute names beyond case id.
cards.answer: Activity, time, costs and resource.
distractors: Place, transition, arc and marking.
Precision, fitness, recall and F1.
Sender, receiver, protocol and port only.

cards.question: Which of these is a possible source of event data for process mining?
cards.answer: Databases, transaction logs, ERP systems, APIs to websites, CSV files and spreadsheets.
distractors: Only process-aware workflow engines.
Only XES files created by process mining tools.
Only hand-drawn process models.

cards.question: The definition of a case is not always fixed a priori. Give an example from the lecture of how this matters.
cards.answer: For an e-mail inbox you may choose the subject as case id, the sender as resource or activity name, and the timestamp as timestamp; other mappings might be meaningful as well.
distractors: E-mails must always be mapped using the body as case id.
An inbox can never be mapped to an event log.
Each e-mail is always an entire case with exactly one event.

cards.question: For e-mail data, why is there no single correct mapping to case id and activity name?
cards.answer: The right mapping depends on the context and on the questions we want to answer.
distractors: Because e-mails have no timestamps.
Because the XES standard forbids a mapping.
Because only the sender can serve as case id.

cards.question: In student exam data where each event is an exam attempt, which choice is plausible for the case id?
cards.answer: The student id, so that a case is the sequence of exam attempts of one student.
distractors: The mark of the exam.
The nationality of the student.
The gender of the student.

cards.question: What is the standard transactional life-cycle of an activity used for?
cards.answer: It describes the states of an activity instance, such as scheduled, started, suspended and completed, so that events can record transitions between states.
distractors: It describes the order of cases in an event log.
It defines how Petri net markings evolve.
It is a method to remove noise from logs.

cards.question: What is the secondary correlation problem for overlapping activity instances?
cards.answer: Besides assigning events to a case, one must also link events (such as start and complete) that belong to the same activity instance, when several instances of the same activity overlap.
distractors: Assigning every event to a resource.
Merging two cases that contain the same activities.
Deciding which events are noise.

cards.question: What solutions does the lecture mention for secondary correlation?
cards.answer: Add more information to the log, or use heuristics such as first-in-first-out matching.
distractors: Delete every overlapping event.
Always use the alpha algorithm.
Convert the log to a Petri net first.

cards.question: What is XES?
cards.answer: The eXtensible Event Stream, an IEEE standard XML-based format for event logs, supported by most commercial and open source tools.
distractors: A graphical notation for Petri nets.
A discovery algorithm for workflow nets.
A query language for relational databases.

cards.question: Can logs be converted between CSV and XES?
cards.answer: Yes; there are possibilities to convert from CSV to XES and vice versa.
distractors: No; XES is only for models.
Only from XES to CSV.
Only if the log has no timestamps.

cards.question: What is noise in an event log, as discussed in the lecture?
cards.answer: Incorrect or unrepresentative recordings, for example from logging that was temporarily unavailable or from rare unusual behavior.
distractors: Any event that has a resource attribute.
The set of all frequent traces.
Events from systems with process awareness.

cards.question: Why is noise a major problem for process mining?
cards.answer: It strongly affects discovery, conformance checking and enhancement, and it is nearly impossible to characterise without domain knowledge.
distractors: It only affects visualization colors.
It only matters for logs with more than one resource.
It improves the precision of discovered models.

cards.question: What assumption underlies log-based noise handling?
cards.answer: Noise is rare, so very infrequent traces, or traces with very infrequent transitions, can be treated as noise.
distractors: Noise is always frequent.
Noise only occurs in the last event of each case.
Noise can be removed by sorting the log alphabetically.

cards.question: Why can the frequency-based noise assumption be wrong?
cards.answer: A rare trace might be legitimate (for example a rare but valid exceptional case) and not noise.
distractors: Because frequent traces are always noise.
Because rare traces never occur in practice.
Because noise cannot be detected by counting.

cards.question: In the noise example, traces ACD 99, ACE 2, BCE 85, BCD 3 are observed. Which traces are probably noise?
cards.answer: ACE and BCD, because they are very infrequent compared with ACD and BCE.
distractors: ACD and BCE, because they are frequent.
None; all traces are equally likely noise.
ACD and BCD, because they end with D.

cards.question: In the noise example with ACD 99, ACE 88, BCE 85, BCD 78, what does the log suggest?
cards.answer: All four combinations occur frequently, so none is noise; the model with a free choice before and after C is appropriate.
distractors: ACE and BCD must be noise.
The log contains no information about choices.
The model must contain a loop.

cards.question: Which practical differences between event logs does the lecture list?
cards.answer: Semantics of timestamps, total versus partial order, and quality such as completeness, noise level and data richness.
distractors: Only the file size and the compression format.
Only the number of activities.
Only whether the log is stored in XES.

cards.question: What is a major issue even when technical alignment of logs by standards is achieved?
cards.answer: Semantic alignment, because the same attribute may mean different things in different sources.
distractors: Choosing a font for the log.
Converting numbers to strings.
Compressing the log file.

cards.question: What are the three quality dimensions for discovered models given in the lecture?
cards.answer: Fitness, precision–generalisation trade-off, and simplicity.
distractors: Speed, memory and energy.
Soundness, safety and liveness.
Completeness, noise and richness.

cards.question: What does fitness of a discovered model mean?
cards.answer: The model should allow for the behavior seen in the log.
distractors: The model should be as small as possible.
The model should allow behavior unrelated to the log.
The model should contain exactly one trace.

cards.question: What is the precision–generalisation trade-off?
cards.answer: The model should not allow behavior completely unrelated to the log (precision), but should generalize to some extent beyond what was seen (generalisation).
distractors: The model should replay only the traces in the log, and nothing else.
The model should allow every sequence of activities.
The model should be as complex as possible.

cards.question: What does simplicity mean as a quality dimension of a discovered model?
cards.answer: The model should be as simple as possible while still describing the behavior.
distractors: The model should have exactly one place.
The model should only contain sequential behavior.
The model should be unreadable to humans.

cards.question: Why is discovery difficult even when a log exists?
cards.answer: Typically not every possible behavior (trace) has been executed and recorded, so the log is only a sample of the process.
distractors: Because logs always contain more behavior than the process allows.
Because logs have no ordering.
Because Petri nets cannot represent logs.

cards.question: A model that allows every possible sequence of the activities replays any log. Which quality dimension does it violate most?
cards.answer: Precision (and simplicity of insight), because it allows behavior that is unrelated to the log.
distractors: Fitness.
Generalisation.
Soundness.

cards.question: A model that contains exactly the traces seen in the log and nothing more has high fitness and precision. Which quality dimension is most at risk?
cards.answer: Generalisation, since unseen but valid behavior is not allowed.
distractors: Fitness.
Precision.
Having a case id.

cards.question: What is the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: A simple process discovery algorithm that builds a workflow net from ordering relations between activities in a workflow log.
distractors: A noise filtering algorithm for XES logs.
A conformance checking method that computes alignments.
An algorithm that builds a log from a Petri net.

cards.question: Why is the alpha algorithm mostly used for illustration rather than practice?
cards.answer: It is easy and has provable properties, but it is not robust against noise or incomplete or erroneous logs.
distractors: It cannot detect any concurrency.
It requires manual drawing of the model.
It only works with logs containing resources.

cards.question: What do the α+ and α++ algorithms do?
cards.answer: They extend the alpha algorithm to discover a broader spectrum of constructs, but they are still not robust against noise.
distractors: They remove all noise from event logs.
They discover models from several logs at once.
They replace Petri nets by LTSs.

cards.question: What is a workflow log in the alpha algorithm setting?
cards.answer: A set W ⊆ T* of distinct traces, with no cardinalities and no case ids.
distractors: A multiset of events with case ids and timestamps.
A set of places and transitions.
A table of resources and costs.

cards.question: What does T* denote?
cards.answer: The set of all finite sequences over the set of activities T.
distractors: The set of transitions with a star.
The set of all places of a net.
The set of infinite loops.

cards.question: What assumption does the alpha algorithm make about activities in the process model?
cards.answer: Each task occurs at most once in the process model (no duplicate tasks).
distractors: Each task occurs exactly twice.
Every task is concurrent with every other.
Tasks have no names.

cards.question: Given the log with cases ABCD, ACBD, ABCD, ACBD and EF, what is the workflow log W?
cards.answer: W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}.
distractors: W = {ABCD, ABCD, ACBD, ACBD, EF}.
W = {A, B, C, D, E, F}.
W = {AB, CD, EF}.

cards.question: Define the direct succession relation x > y in a workflow log W.
cards.answer: x > y holds iff in at least one trace x is directly followed by y.
distractors: x > y holds iff x occurs before y anywhere in some trace.
x > y holds iff x occurs more often than y.
x > y holds iff x and y never occur in the same trace.

cards.question: Define causality x → y in a workflow log.
cards.answer: x → y iff x > y and not y > x.
distractors: x → y iff x > y and y > x.
x → y iff not x > y and not y > x.
x → y iff x and y occur in the same trace.

cards.question: Define the parallel relation x || y in a workflow log.
cards.answer: x || y iff x > y and y > x.
distractors: x || y iff x > y and not y > x.
x || y iff not x > y and not y > x.
x || y iff x and y never occur together.

cards.question: Define the choice relation x # y in a workflow log.
cards.answer: x # y iff not x > y and not y > x.
distractors: x # y iff x > y and y > x.
x # y iff x → y.
x # y iff x occurs in more traces than y.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, which direct succession relations hold for A?
cards.answer: A > B and A > C.
distractors: A > D only.
A > E and A > F.
B > A and C > A.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, which of these causal relations holds?
cards.answer: A → B, A → C, B → D, C → D and E → F.
distractors: B → C and C → B.
A → E and A → F.
D → A.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, which pair is in the parallel relation?
cards.answer: B || C (and C || B).
distractors: A || B.
E || F.
A || D.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, is A # E true?
cards.answer: Yes; A and E never directly follow each other in either order.
distractors: No; A > E in the log.
No; E → A.
Only if E occurs before A.

cards.question: Is x # x possible, and what does it mean for A in W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}?
cards.answer: Yes; A # A holds because A never directly follows itself.
distractors: No; every task directly follows itself.
Only for the final transition.
It means A is parallel to itself.

cards.question: What is the difference between x → y and x > y?
cards.answer: x > y only says that y directly follows x at least once; x → y additionally requires that y never directly precedes x.
distractors: x → y is weaker than x > y.
x > y requires that x and y are in choice.
They are the same relation.

cards.question: How can you tell from the log that two tasks are parallel and not in a choice?
cards.answer: Parallel tasks are observed in both orders as direct successors; tasks in choice never directly follow each other.
distractors: Parallel tasks never occur in the same log.
Tasks in choice occur in both orders.
Parallel tasks always occur in the same order.

cards.question: What is the basic idea of the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: Create a workflow net from the ordering relations such that the ordering is obeyed, by deriving a Petri net fragment from each relation.
distractors: Compute the shortest path through all traces.
Train a classifier on the traces.
Align each trace with a reference model.

cards.question: How does the alpha algorithm obtain the set of transitions T_W?
cards.answer: As the set of all tasks that appear in at least one trace of W.
distractors: As the set of tasks that appear in every trace.
As the set of tasks that appear first in some trace.
As the set of places with tokens.

cards.question: What are T_I and T_O in the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: T_I is the set of tasks that appear first in some trace; T_O is the set of tasks that appear last in some trace.
distractors: T_I is the set of inputs of the log; T_O its outputs.
T_I is the set of tasks in choice; T_O the set of tasks in parallel.
T_I is the set of tasks occurring once; T_O the set of tasks occurring more than once.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, what are T_I and T_O?
cards.answer: T_I = {A, E} and T_O = {D, F}.
distractors: T_I = {A} and T_O = {D}.
T_I = {A, E} and T_O = {B, C}.
T_I = {A, B} and T_O = {E, F}.

cards.question: What is the set X_W in the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: The set of pairs (A, B) of non-empty task sets such that every a ∈ A causally precedes every b ∈ B, and all tasks in A are pairwise in choice, and all tasks in B are pairwise in choice.
distractors: The set of pairs of tasks that are in parallel.
The set of all subsets of T_W.
The set of pairs (a, b) with a > b.

cards.question: What is the set Y_W in the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: The pairs (A, B) in X_W that are maximal: no other pair in X_W contains both A and B in larger sets.
distractors: The pairs in X_W with the fewest tasks.
The pairs in X_W where A and B are singletons.
All pairs in X_W that include the start task.

cards.question: Why is the maximality condition in Y_W needed?
cards.answer: It removes redundant places that are implied by larger pairs, so each place is created only for the maximal pair.
distractors: It ensures that parallel tasks are in choice.
It adds the initial and final places.
It makes the log complete.

cards.question: How are the places P_W of α(W) defined?
cards.answer: One place p(A,B) for each pair (A,B) in Y_W, plus an input place i_W and an output place o_W.
distractors: One place for each task in T_W.
One place for each trace in W.
One place for each pair of parallel tasks.

cards.question: How is the flow relation F_W of α(W) defined?
cards.answer: Arcs a → p(A,B) for a ∈ A, arcs p(A,B) → b for b ∈ B, arcs from i_W to every t ∈ T_I, and arcs from every t ∈ T_O to o_W.
distractors: Arcs only between tasks that are parallel.
Arcs from i_W to all tasks and from all tasks to o_W.
Arcs between places only.

cards.question: What is the output of the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: A workflow net α(W) = (P_W, T_W, F_W).
distractors: An LTS with labelled transitions.
A set of ordering relations.
A filtered event log.

cards.question: For L1 = [⟨a,b,c,d⟩³, ⟨a,c,b,d⟩², ⟨a,e,d⟩], what causal and parallel relations hold?
cards.answer: a→b, a→c, a→e, b→d, c→d, e→d, and b || c.
distractors: a→d and b→c.
b→e and c→e.
b # c and e || d.

cards.question: For L1 = [⟨a,b,c,d⟩³, ⟨a,c,b,d⟩², ⟨a,e,d⟩], which pairs (A,B) form the places in Y_W?
distractors: ({a,e},{d}) only.

cards.question: For L1, why is ({a},{b,c}) not a valid pair in X_W?
cards.answer: Because b and c are parallel, not in choice, so they cannot be together in the output set B.
distractors: Because a is not causally followed by b.
Because b and c never occur in the log.
Because a occurs only once.

cards.question: In L2, every trace starts with a and ends with d, and b and c always occur together without a particular order. What does the discovered model likely show?
cards.answer: a as the only start, d as the only end, and b and c in parallel (AND split and join).
distractors: b and c in an exclusive choice.
b and c in a loop of length one.
a occurring after d.

cards.question: In L2, every e is followed by an f and every f is preceded by an e. What does this indicate for the model?
cards.answer: e and f are tightly coupled in sequence, forming a block that can be repeated in a loop.
distractors: e and f are parallel to each other.
e and f are in exclusive choice.
f can occur without e.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, how many places does α(W) have?
distractors: Five.
Six.
Eight.

cards.question: For W = {ABCD, ACBD, EF}, what does α(W) look like?
cards.answer: Two disconnected fragments sharing i_W and o_W: A splits in parallel into B and C which join in D, and E followed by F via its own place.
distractors: A single sequence A, B, C, D, E, F.
An exclusive choice between A and E, then B, C, D, F in parallel.
A loop from D back to A.

cards.question: What kind of log completeness does the alpha algorithm require?
cards.answer: Completeness with respect to the direct succession relation: whenever two tasks may occur as direct successors, this must be observed in at least one trace.
distractors: Every possible trace must appear in the log.
Every trace must appear at least ten times.
Every task must appear in every trace.

cards.question: Why does the alpha completeness criterion help for highly concurrent processes?
cards.answer: It requires only that each pair of direct successors is seen, so far fewer traces are needed than all interleavings.
distractors: It requires all interleavings, which are easy to observe.
It ignores concurrency.
It requires only one trace.

cards.question: Five tasks A to E run concurrently. The log has ABCDE and BACED. Is BACDE required for completeness?
cards.answer: No; every direct succession it contains is already observed in the other traces, so it is not required.
distractors: Yes; all permutations must be observed.
Yes; every trace of length five must appear.
No; because ordering is irrelevant to alpha.

cards.question: What is the rediscovery problem?
cards.answer: For which class of workflow nets WF1 can we guarantee that mining a complete log of WF1 returns a net WF2 that is equivalent to WF1.
distractors: How to rediscover a lost event log from a model.
How to discover a model without any log.
How to rediscover noise in a log.

cards.question: Which nets can the alpha algorithm rediscover?
cards.answer: Sound structured workflow nets without short loops, if the log is complete with respect to the direct succession relation.
distractors: All workflow nets, if the log is complete.
Only sequential nets without any choice.
Any Petri net with implicit places.

cards.question: What is an implicit place?
cards.answer: A place whose presence or absence does not change the behavior of the net system.
distractors: A place with no tokens.
A place that is the initial place i.
A place with more than one outgoing arc.

cards.question: Why can models with implicit places not be rediscovered, and why is this not a big problem?
cards.answer: The log cannot reveal them since they do not affect behavior, but since they have no consequences for behavior, nothing is lost.
distractors: They change the traces of the model, so they are noise.
They make the net unsound.
They cause the log to be incomplete.

cards.question: What is a structured workflow net (SWF-net)?
cards.answer: A WF-net with no implicit places such that for arcs (p,t): |p•|>1 implies |•t|=1 (no mixing choice and synchronization), and |•t|>1 implies |•p|=1.
distractors: A WF-net with exactly one path from i to o.
A WF-net with only one transition.
A WF-net without any concurrency.

cards.question: What does the SWF-net restriction 'for (p,t) ∈ F, |p•|>1 implies |•t|=1' forbid?
cards.answer: A choice place whose chosen transition also has to synchronize with other input places (mixing choice and synchronization).
distractors: Any place with several tokens.
Any transition with more than one output place.
Any parallel split.

cards.question: Can an SWF-net express sequences, concurrency and exclusive choices?
cards.answer: Yes; it is expressive enough for most process control-flow structures.
distractors: No; it can only express sequences.
No; it cannot express concurrency.
No; it cannot express choices.

cards.question: What is soundness of a workflow net?
cards.answer: A behavioral correctness criterion: the process terminates in a proper final state, the final state is unambiguous, and all activities can contribute to executions.
distractors: A structural criterion saying every place has at least one token.
A criterion saying the net has no choices.
A criterion saying the net is bipartite.

cards.question: What does the 'option to complete' condition of soundness say?
cards.answer: For every marking M reachable from i, there is a firing sequence from M to the final marking o.
distractors: Every transition fires exactly once.
The net can reach o from i only through one path.
The net has no deadlocks at the initial marking only.

cards.question: What does the 'proper completion' condition of soundness say?
cards.answer: The marking o is the only reachable marking with a token in place o, so no tokens remain elsewhere when o is marked.
distractors: Place o can never be marked.
Place o must always contain two tokens.
Every reachable marking has a token in o.

cards.question: What does the 'no dead transitions' condition of soundness say?
cards.answer: For every transition t, there is a reachable marking from i in which t is enabled and can fire.
distractors: Every transition is enabled in the initial marking.
Every transition fires in every trace.
Transitions cannot have output places.

cards.question: What does 'i' and 'o' denote as markings in the soundness definition?
cards.answer: i is the marking with one token in place i and nothing elsewhere; o is the marking with one token in place o and nothing elsewhere.
distractors: i and o are numbers of tokens in the net.
i and o are the first and last transitions.
i and o are the sets of input and output places.

cards.question: A WF-net can reach a marking [o, p] with two marked places. Which soundness condition is violated?
cards.answer: Proper completion, since o is marked while another place also holds a token.
distractors: Option to complete.
No dead transitions.
Strong connectedness.

cards.question: A WF-net can reach a marking from which o cannot be reached any more. Which soundness condition is violated?
cards.answer: Option to complete.
distractors: Proper completion.
No dead transitions.
Bipartiteness.

cards.question: Why are short loops a problem for the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: Loops of length one or two produce direct successions in both directions, so the tasks look parallel and the corresponding loop structure is not rediscovered correctly.
distractors: Short loops are not allowed in logs.
Short loops remove the initial place.
Short loops add implicit places.

cards.question: What are short loops, in the alpha algorithm context?
cards.answer: Loops of length 1 or 2 in the process model.
distractors: Loops with at most one token.
Loops that occur at most twice in a log.
Loops of length three or more.

cards.question: Why is a length-two loop between b and c (trace abcbcd) misinterpreted by the alpha algorithm?
cards.answer: Both b > c and c > b occur, so b || c is concluded instead of a loop.
distractors: b # c is concluded.
b and c are not seen at all.
The algorithm sees c → b only.

cards.question: What is the difference between the alpha algorithm and its rediscovery guarantee?
cards.answer: The algorithm can be run on any log, but it is only guaranteed to return an equivalent model for sound structured WF-nets without short loops given a log that is complete w.r.t. direct succession.
distractors: The algorithm works only on complete logs.
The guarantee holds for all workflow nets.
The guarantee holds for all noisy logs.

cards.question: What distinguishes α-algorithm discovery from conformance checking in terms of inputs?
cards.answer: Discovery takes only a log; conformance checking takes a log and a model.
distractors: Discovery takes a model and a log; conformance takes only a log.
Both take only a model.
Both take only a log.
